Notes: Web_Programming- Component life cycle

Component life cycle
In this topic, we will learn about how a component goes through the different phases in its life cycle. These different phases are associated with some callback functions which can be used for performing some specific task
Overview
​​​​​​​
​
Each component in React has a lifecycle which you can monitor and manipulate during its three main phases.
The three phases are: Mounting, Updating, and Unmounting.
Each component has several lifecycle methods that you can override to run code at particular times in the process. There are some frequently used methods in the life cycle like componentDidMount(). The rest of them exist for relatively rare use cases.
Mounting phase
When an instance of a component is being created and inserted into the DOM it is considered as mounting phase of component's life cycle. Following methods are called in the same sequence the way are written.
  1. constructor()
  2. static getDerivedStateFromProps()
  3. render()
  4. componentDidMount()
The render() method is required and will always be called, the others are optional and will be called if they are defined
constructor() method
It is called before anything else, when the component is initiated, and it is the natural place to set up the initial state and other initial values.
The constructor() method is called with the props, as arguments, and you should always start by calling the super(props) before anything else. When we call this super(props), we are basically calling the constructor of React.Component. If this keyword is needed to be used inside the child class constructor, we need to pass the props coming from the parent class in super.
static getDerivedStateFromProps()
It is called just before calling the render() method.
This is a static function that does not have access to 'this'.  getDerivedStateFromProps() returns an object to update state in response to prop changes. It can return a null if there is no change to state.
This method also exists only for rare use cases where the state depends on changes in props in a component.
render()
The render() method is the most used lifecycle method. render() is the only required method within a class component in React. 
As the name suggests it handles the rendering of the component to the UI. Rendering takes place during the mounting and updating of the component.
the render() method returns JSX that is displayed in the UI. A render() can also return a null if there is nothing to render for that component.
componentDidMount()
componentDidMount() is called as soon as the component is mounted and ready. This is a good place to initiate API calls, if you need to load data from a remote endpoint.
Unlike the render() method, componentDidMount() allows the use of setState(). Calling the setState() here will update state and cause another rendering but it will happen before the browser updates the UI. 
Example
class Header extends React.Component {
  constructor(props) {
    super(props);
    this.state = {emps: []};
  }
  componentDidMount() {
   //may give call to REST API to fetch data
  }
  render() {
    return (
      <h1>List of employees </h1>
      //display the list of employees
    );
  }
}


Updating phase
After mouting phase, the next phase in the lifecycle is when a component is updated. A component is updated whenever there is a change in the component's state or props.
React has five built-in methods that gets called, in the following order, when a component is updated:
  1. getDerivedStateFromProps()
  2. shouldComponentUpdate()
  3. render()
  4. getSnapshotBeforeUpdate()
  5. componentDidUpdate()
The render() method is required and will always be called, the others are optional and will be called if you define them.
getDerivedStateFromProps()
During update phase even, the getDerivedStateFromProps method is called. This is the first method that is called when a component gets updated.
shouldComponentUpdate()
Anytime setState() is called, the component re-renders by default. The shouldComponentUpdate() method is used to make React understand if a component is not affected by the state and prop changes.
This lifecycle method should be very rarely used, and it exists only for certain performance optimizations. You cannot update component state in shouldComponentUpdate() lifecycle.
In the shouldComponentUpdate() method you can return a Boolean value that specifies whether React should continue with the rendering or not. The default value is true.
Render()
The render() method is of course called when a component gets updated, it has to re-render the HTML to the DOM, with the new changes.
getSnapshotBeforeUpdate()
getSnapshotBeforeUpdate() is another new lifecycle method introduced in React recently.
It is called right before the DOM is updated. The value that is returned from getSnapshotBeforeUpdate() is passed on to componentDidUpdate().
This method should also be used rarely or not used at all.
Resizing the window during an async rendering is a good use-case of when the getSnapshotBeforeUpdate() can be utilized.
componentDidUpdate()
This lifecycle method is invoked as soon as the updating happens. The most common use case for the componentDidUpdate() method is updating the DOM in response to prop or state changes.
setState() method can be called in this lifecycle only if state or prop have been modified from previous state. Incorrect usage of setState() in this method can lead to an infinite loop.
Unmounting Phase
The next phase in the lifecycle is when a component is removed from the DOM, or unmounting as called by React. 
React has only one built-in method that gets called when a component is unmounted:
componentWillUnmount().
componentWillUnmount()
As the name suggests this lifecycle method is called just before the component is unmounted and destroyed. If there are any cleanup actions that you would need to do, this would be the right location. Best example of actions that can be written in this method is clearing the page refreshes that are set.
This component will never be re-rendered and because of that we cannot call setState() during this lifecycle method.
useEffect hook
​​​​​​​useEffect() hook accepts 2 arguments:
useEffect(callback[, dependencies]);
callback is a function that contains the side-effect logic. callback is executed right after the DOM update.
dependencies is an optional array of dependencies. Following are the different use cases for this hook.
  1. When dependencies update
    useEffect(
        () => {
            // execute side effect
        },
        // optional dependency array
        [
            // 1 or more entries
        ] 
    )
    useEffect() executes callback only if the dependencies have changed between renderings.
  2. When component renders for the first time
    It is even possible to  send an empty array as second argument. 
    useEffect(() => { 
        // execute side effect
    },[])
    This effect will run only after first render that means after mounting of the component
  3. When component renders as well as dependencies update
    useEffect(() => { 
        // execute side effect
    })
    By using this Hook, you tell React that your component needs to do something after render. React will remember the function you passed (we’ll refer to it as our “effect”), and call it later after performing the DOM updates. By default, it runs both after the first render and after every update.

Note following points
  • Instead of thinking in terms of “mounting” and “updating”, you might find it easier to think that effects happen “after render”.
  • The following steps are carried out for a functional React component if at least one effect is defined:
    The component will be re-rendered based on a state, prop, or context change
    If one or more useEffect declarations exist for the component, React checks each useEffect to determine whether it fulfills the conditions to execute the implementation (the body of the callback function provided as first argument). In this case, “conditions” mean one or more dependencies have changed since the last render cycle
  • Dependencies are array items provided as the optional second argument of the useEffect call. Array values must be from the component scope (i.e., props, state, context, or values derived from any of it):

Example
useEffect ( ()=> {
         const timer = setInterval( ()=>{setCurdate(new Date())}, 1000);            
         return ()=> { clearInterval(timer)}
        },[]
    )
Note : Above effect gets called after first render and sets the date to current date. It sets a referesh which gets executed after 1000 ms. 'return' Statement added gets executed after before component is unmounted.
​
